title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 5.3.1 Grammar in Use: Word Classes (Adjectives)

PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Adjectives describe people, food and objects. In this sub-strand you will find adjectives in a text, use the comparative forms of regular and irregular adjectives, and put adjectives of size and shape in the right order when you talk about meals and kitchen things.

## Strand 5.0: Nutrition - Balanced Diet
Sub-strand 5.3.1: Grammar in Use: Word Classes (Adjectives)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: communication
b) use adjectives of size and shape in the right order for clarity of communication
c) adopt the use of adjectives for effective communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Regular adjectives
• Irregular Adjectives

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we say the correct shape and size of things?
2. Which are some of the words you use to talk about how someone feels or looks?
3. How do we describe things?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is developed as the learner uses adjectives correctly in sentences as they interact with peers.
• Self-efficacy is developed as the learner is able to gain confidence as they use adjectives accurately in their day-to-day communication.

## Values
• Unity: It is promoted as learners cohesively relate with each other to perform activities such as identifying and discussing adjectives.
• Responsibility: This is cultivated as the learner takes personal initiative to complete assigned roles.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Health Education: This is promoted as the learner gets information on lifestyle diseases through the theme of balanced diet

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to connect the concept of comparative adjectives to the learning of adjectives in English and Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 5.0 Nutrition – Balanced Diet, Sub-strand 5.3.1 Word Classes: Adjectives

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Finding adjectives and regular comparatives

LESSON 1: FINDING ADJECTIVES AND REGULAR COMPARATIVES
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• Pick out adjectives from a short text about food.
• Form the comparative and superlative of regular adjectives.
• Use than when comparing two things.

Curriculum outcomes: a) By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: communication

## Introduction
A mango is a noun. Ripe tells us something about that mango. Without adjectives, a shopping list is only a line of names. With them, we can say which fruit is fresh, which pot is large, and which meal is healthier.

## Notes
### What an adjective does
An adjective describes a noun or a pronoun. It often sits just before the noun, or after is, are, was or were.

- a sweet mango (before the noun)
- The mango is sweet. (after is)

Colour, size, shape, taste and how healthy something is can all be adjectives: red, small, round, juicy, fresh, balanced.

Read this text and listen for describing words.

The cook carried a large round tray. On it sat fresh beans, a juicy mango and a small square tin of groundnuts. 'This meal is healthier than tea and sweets,' she said. The hungry pupils agreed that the mango smelled sweet.

The adjectives include large, round, fresh, juicy, small, square, healthier, hungry and sweet. Tray, beans, mango, tin, meal and pupils are nouns.

### Regular comparatives
When we compare, many adjectives take a regular pattern.

- Short adjectives usually add -er and -est: sweet, sweeter, sweetest; fresh, fresher, freshest; small, smaller, smallest.
- An adjective ending in e adds -r and -st: large, larger, largest.
- A short adjective ending in one vowel plus one consonant doubles the consonant: big, bigger, biggest; thin, thinner, thinnest.
- An adjective ending in a consonant plus y changes y to i: healthy, healthier, healthiest; juicy, juicier, juiciest.
- A longer adjective uses more and most: more balanced, most balanced; more delicious, most delicious.

Use than between the two things: This orange is sweeter than that one. Use the when you mean the winner of a whole group: She chose the freshest bunch.

Plump and thin can describe size, but do not aim them at a classmate as a joke. Compare fruit and tins, or speak kindly about health: a more balanced meal, a healthier habit.

## Key words
• adjective — a word that describes a noun, such as fresh, round or healthy
• comparative — the form of an adjective used to compare two things, such as sweeter or more balanced
• superlative — the form used to compare more than two, such as sweetest or most balanced
• regular adjective — an adjective whose comparative follows a usual spelling rule, such as adding -er or using more

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Write the comparative and superlative of healthy.

Working:
1. Healthy ends in a consonant plus y.
2. Change y to i, then add -er or -est.

Answer: healthier, healthiest

### Example 2
Complete: This mango is ____ (juicy) than the banana.

Working:
1. Compare two fruits, so use the comparative.
2. Juicy becomes juicier.

Answer: This mango is juicier than the banana.

## Activity: Adjectives in the classroom
You will need: Classroom objects such as a book, a tin, a bottle and a piece of fruit if one is available, The short tray paragraph
1. Read the paragraph aloud. Each learner underlines two adjectives and circles the nouns they describe.
2. Choose two classroom objects and compare them with a regular adjective: The blue book is smaller than the atlas.
3. Write three sentences using -er or more, each with the word than.
4. Check spellings: bigger, healthier, more balanced.

## Practice
1. Is 'beans' an adjective in 'fresh beans'? What is the adjective?
2. Write the comparative of big and of large.
3. Make a sentence comparing two fruits with tastier.
4. When do we use more instead of -er?

## Summary
• Adjectives describe nouns.
• Regular comparatives use -er, -est or more and most, with spelling changes you can learn.
• Use than to compare two things.

### Answers to practice
1. No. Beans is the noun. Fresh is the adjective.
2. bigger; larger
3. The mango is tastier than the lemon. Any correct sentence with tastier than is acceptable.
4. With longer adjectives, such as more delicious or more balanced.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Irregular adjectives

LESSON 2: IRREGULAR ADJECTIVES
==============================

## What you will learn
• Use good, bad, many, much, little and far in their irregular forms.
• Choose a regular or an irregular comparative to match the adjective.
• Compare foods without unkind comments about people's bodies.

Curriculum outcomes: a) By the end of the Sub Strand, the learner should be able to: communication; b) use adjectives of size and shape in the right order for clarity of communication

## Introduction
Good does not become gooder. If you say it, the listener still understands you, but the sentence sounds unfinished. A few common adjectives keep their own forms, and those forms have to be remembered.

## Notes
### The irregular set
These adjectives do not add -er or -est.

- good, better, best
- bad, worse, worst
- many, more, most
- much, more, most
- little, less, least (when little means a small amount)
- far, farther, farthest

Many goes with things you can count: many oranges, more oranges, the most oranges. Much goes with things you do not count one by one: much sugar, more sugar, the most sugar. Little here means a small amount, not a small object. There is less sugar in this tea than in that cup.

Farther is about distance: The market is farther than the school farm.

### Regular beside irregular
Fresh is regular: fresher fruit. Good is irregular: better fruit, not gooder fruit. Bad is irregular: worse, not badder. A long regular adjective still uses more: more careful, not carefuller.

### Sentences about meals
- Beans are better body-building food than sweets.
- Too much sugar is worse for teeth than a piece of fruit.
- This jug has less water than that one.
- Of the three stalls, Grandmother's has the best spinach.
- We should buy more fruit and less oil when the bottle is still half full.

Do not say a person is 'the worst body' or 'less of a friend' because of their size. Compare the food and the habit. If you are worried that someone is ill, tell an adult.

### A quick test you can say aloud
Ask: am I comparing two things, or a whole group? Two things take the middle form: better, worse, more, less, farther. A whole group takes the last form, usually with the: the best, the worst, the most, the least, the farthest.

## Key words
• irregular adjective — an adjective whose comparative does not follow the usual -er ending, such as good, better, best
• amount — how much of something there is
• least — the smallest amount
• farther — at or to a greater distance

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Complete: This meal is ____ (good) than yesterday's meal.

Working:
1. Good is irregular.
2. The comparative is better, followed by than.

Answer: This meal is better than yesterday's meal.

### Example 2
Choose many or much: We need ____ spinach and ____ tomatoes.

Working:
1. Spinach is treated as a food we do not count leaf by leaf in this sentence, so much or more can fit, but the usual school contrast is much sugar, many tomatoes.
2. Tomatoes can be counted, so many.

Answer: We need more spinach and many tomatoes. Or: much spinach and many tomatoes.

## Activity: Better, worse, more, less
You will need: Cards printed with good, bad, many, much, little, far, Pictures of two meals
1. Turn over a card and say all three forms, for example bad, worse, worst.
2. With a partner, describe two meal pictures using better, worse, more or less.
3. Write four sentences. Two must use irregular adjectives and the word than.
4. Read them aloud and let the group catch any 'gooder' or 'badder'.

## Practice
1. Write the three forms of bad.
2. Complete: Of all the drinks, clean water is the ____ (good) choice with a meal.
3. Which is correct: 'less sugar' or 'fewer sugar'?
4. Give the comparative of far.

## Summary
• Good, bad, many, much, little and far have special forms.
• Use better, worse, more, less and farther when you compare two things.
• Compare food and habits kindly.

### Answers to practice
1. bad, worse, worst
2. best
3. less sugar, because sugar is an amount we are not counting as separate items.
4. farther

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Adjectives of size and shape in order

LESSON 3: ADJECTIVES OF SIZE AND SHAPE IN ORDER
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Place a size adjective before a shape adjective.
• Use a comparative of size or shape without mixing up the order.
• Describe a picture of food with adjectives in a clear sentence.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use adjectives of size and shape in the right order for clarity of communication; c) adopt the use of adjectives for effective communication

## Introduction
People say a big round chapati. They do not usually say a round big chapati. Both words describe the chapati, but English has a preferred order, and size comes before shape.

## Notes
### Size, then shape
Size answers how big something is: tiny, small, little, big, large, long, short, tall.
Shape answers what outline it has: round, square, oval, flat, triangular.

When both appear before a noun, say the size first and the shape second.

- a big round chapati
- a small oval egg
- a large square tin
- a long thin bean pod
- a tiny round orange

You do not need a comma between these two adjectives in ordinary sentences.

### Add a comparative carefully
You can compare the size and still keep the shape in the right place.

- This is a bigger round tray than that one.
- She chose the smaller square tin.
- The oval plate is larger than the square plate.

In the last sentence, shape words sit in two noun phrases, and larger is the comparative of size. That is correct because each phrase has its own order.

Avoid a round bigger tray. The ear expects the size word before the shape word.

### Describing a picture
Look at a market picture and build one clear sentence, not a pile of adjectives.

On the left there is a large round basket of mangoes. Beside it is a small square box of tomatoes. The round watermelons are bigger than the oranges. The stall looks fuller than the one across the path.

Fuller is a regular comparative. Bigger is the comparative of big, with the doubled g. They can live in the same description if each sentence stays tidy.

### Make it a habit
Before you speak, tap two fingers: first finger for size, second for shape. If you only have one adjective, use it. Do not add an empty word. 'A round orange' is enough when you are not talking about size. Clear description helps someone else find the right tin, fruit or plate.

## Key words
• size — how big or small something is
• shape — the outline of something, such as round, square or oval
• order of adjectives — the usual sequence of describing words before a noun
• oval — shaped like an egg, rounded but longer than a circle

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put the adjectives in order: a (round, large) basket.

Working:
1. Large is size. Round is shape.
2. Size comes before shape.

Answer: a large round basket

### Example 2
Correct: She bought a square smaller tin.

Working:
1. Smaller is the comparative of size.
2. Square is the shape and should follow the size word.

Answer: She bought a smaller square tin.

## Activity: Describe the picture in order
You will need: A picture, comic or drawing of a kitchen or market, Slips of paper with size words and shape words
1. Sort the slips into a size pile and a shape pile.
2. In pairs, build five phrases: size, then shape, then a noun from the picture.
3. Write three full sentences. At least one must use a comparative such as bigger, smaller or larger.
4. If a tablet is available, type your best sentence and read it to the class.

## Practice
1. Which phrase is in the right order: 'a round big pot' or 'a big round pot'?
2. Join small and oval with the noun 'egg'.
3. Rewrite: He carried a round bigger tray.
4. Write a sentence that compares two plates and uses a shape word.

## Summary
• Say size before shape: a small square tin.
• Comparatives such as bigger still come before the shape word.
• Use adjectives to help someone picture the real object.

### Answers to practice
1. a big round pot
2. a small oval egg
3. He carried a bigger round tray.
4. The round plate is larger than the square plate. Any correct sentence with size order and a comparison is acceptable.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 5.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: WORD CLASSES (ADJECTIVES)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word is an adjective in 'fresh beans'?
   A. fresh
   B. beans
   C. both are adjectives
   D. neither

2. The comparative of healthy is
   A. healthyer
   B. more healthyer
   C. healthier
   D. healthyest

3. The superlative of big is
   A. bigger
   B. biggest
   C. most big
   D. bigest

4. Choose the irregular comparative of good.
   A. gooder
   B. more good
   C. better
   D. bestest

5. There is ____ sugar in this tea than in that one.
   A. fewer
   B. less
   C. leastest
   D. littleer

6. Which sentence is correct?
   A. This fruit is worser than that one.
   B. This fruit is worse than that one.
   C. This fruit is baddest than that one.
   D. This fruit is badder than that one.

7. Which phrase uses size and shape in the right order?
   A. a round large basket
   B. a large round basket
   C. a basket round large
   D. a round basket large

8. Correct the phrase 'a square smaller tin'.
   A. a smaller square tin
   B. a square more small tin
   C. a tin smaller square
   D. a small square more tin

9. Why do we bother about adjective order?
   A. So descriptions are clear and natural
   B. So we can tease people about their size
   C. So nouns disappear
   D. So we avoid all describing words

10. Write a phrase for a tiny egg that is oval.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 5.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: WORD CLASSES (ADJECTIVES)
========================================

1. A. fresh
   Fresh describes the noun beans.

2. C. healthier
   Y changes to i before -er.

3. B. biggest
   Big doubles the g and adds -est.

4. C. better
   Good, better, best is irregular.

5. B. less
   Less is the comparative of little when we mean an amount.

6. B. This fruit is worse than that one.
   The comparative of bad is worse.

7. B. a large round basket
   Size comes before shape, and both come before the noun.

8. A. a smaller square tin
   The size word smaller comes before the shape word square.

9. A. So descriptions are clear and natural
   The right order makes the picture in the sentence easy to follow.

10. a tiny oval egg
   Tiny is the size and oval is the shape.

LESSON 1: FINDING ADJECTIVES AND REGULAR COMPARATIVES
=====================================================

• Form the comparative and superlative of regular adjectives.

LESSON 2: IRREGULAR ADJECTIVES
==============================

## What you will learn
• Use good, bad, many, much, little and far in their irregular forms.
• Choose a regular or an irregular comparative to match the adjective.

- many, more, most
- much, more, most
- little, less, least (when little means a small amount)
- far, farther, farthest

• amount — how much of something there is
• least — the smallest amount
• farther — at or to a greater distance

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Complete: This meal is ____ (good) than yesterday's meal.

Working:
1. Good is irregular.
2. The comparative is better, followed by than.

### Example 2

• Use better, worse, more, less and farther when you compare two things.
• Compare food and habits kindly.

### Answers to practice
1. bad, worse, worst
2. best
3. less sugar, because sugar is an amount we are not counting as separate items.
4. farther

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Adjectives of size and shape in order
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: ADJECTIVES OF SIZE AND SHAPE IN ORDER
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Place a size adjective before a shape adjective.
• Use a comparative of size or shape without mixing up the order.
• Describe a picture of food with adjectives in a clear sentence.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use adjectives of size and shape in the right order for clarity of communication; c) adopt the use of adjectives for effective communication

## Introduction
People say a big round chapati. They do not usually say a round big chapati. Both words describe the chapati, but English has a preferred order, and size comes before shape.

## Notes
### Size, then shape
Size answers how big something is: tiny, small, little, big, large, long, short, tall.
Shape answers what outline it has: round, square, oval, flat, triangular.

When both appear before a noun, say the size first and the shape second.

- a big round chapati
- a small oval egg
- a large square tin
- a long thin bean pod
- a tiny round orange

You do not need a comma between these two adjectives in ordinary sentences.

### Add a comparative carefully
You can compare the size and still keep the shape in the right place.

- This is a bigger round tray than that one.
- She chose the smaller square tin.
- The oval plate is larger than the square plate.

In the last sentence, shape words sit in two noun phrases, and larger is the comparative of size. That is correct because each phrase has its own order.

Avoid a round bigger tray. The ear expects the size word before the shape word.

### Describing a picture
Look at a market picture and build one clear sentence, not a pile of adjectives.

On the left there is a large round basket of mangoes. Beside it is a small square box of tomatoes. The round watermelons are bigger than the oranges. The stall looks fuller than the one across the path.

Fuller is a regular comparative. Bigger is the comparative of big, with the doubled g. They can live in the same description if each sentence stays tidy.

### Make it a habit
Before you speak, tap two fingers: first finger for size, second for shape. If you only have one adjective, use it. Do not add an empty word. 'A round orange' is enough when you are not talking about size. Clear description helps someone else find the right tin, fruit or plate.

## Key words
• size — how big or small something is
• shape — the outline of something, such as round, square or oval
• order of adjectives — the usual sequence of describing words before a noun
• oval — shaped like an egg, rounded but longer than a circle

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put the adjectives in order: a (round, large) basket.

Working:
1. Large is size. Round is shape.
2. Size comes before shape.

Answer: a large round basket

### Example 2
Correct: She bought a square smaller tin.

Working:
1. Smaller is the comparative of size.
2. Square is the shape and should follow the size word.

Answer: She bought a smaller square tin.

## Activity: Describe the picture in order
You will need: A picture, comic or drawing of a kitchen or market, Slips of paper with size words and shape words
1. Sort the slips into a size pile and a shape pile.
2. In pairs, build five phrases: size, then shape, then a noun from the picture.
3. Write three full sentences. At least one must use a comparative such as bigger, smaller or larger.
4. If a tablet is available, type your best sentence and read it to the class.

## Practice
1. Which phrase is in the right order: 'a round big pot' or 'a big round pot'?
2. Join small and oval with the noun 'egg'.
3. Rewrite: He carried a round bigger tray.
4. Write a sentence that compares two plates and uses a shape word.

## Summary
• Say size before shape: a small square tin.
• Comparatives such as bigger still come before the shape word.
• Use adjectives to help someone picture the real object.

### Answers to practice
1. a big round pot
2. a small oval egg
3. He carried a bigger round tray.
4. The round plate is larger than the square plate. Any correct sentence with size order and a comparison is acceptable.
